content:
A def returning a class should now be marked @[implicit_reducible], and there is even a (core) linter to enforce this. However, this doesn't make sense for irreducible_def, but the linter still fires:

import Mathlib

class Foo (α : Type) where
  a : α

irreducible_def myFooNat : Foo ℕ := ⟨0⟩  -- linter complains

Marking the definition as @[implicit_reducible] fails. Is there a way to make sure that the linter doesn't fire on those definitions?

You can use set_option warn.classDefReducibility false in.

It is really annoying that the linter warning does not give this information.
Or did you mean to ask what you should do to remove the set_option?
Yes, I know I can desactivate the linter by hand. But we should rather make sure that it doesn't fire there.
(I'm trying to kill all the uses of set_option warn.classDefReducibility false in Mathlib, and the last remaining ones are of this form)

What is also curious is that the inferInstanceAs elaborator creates definitions that the linter would complain about if you wrote them by hand. So there are genuinely use cases where you don't want your instance to be implicit_reducible.

Sure, but these are the cases where we are abusing defeqs. Users are not supposed to do that, so I think it is nice this is allowed for tools that have been thoroughly thought through, and discouraged for users.

Do you think we should modify irreducible_def, or change the linter so that it will accept irreducible instances in general? I think there could be situations where you really want an instance to be irreducible (and irreducible_def is just a stronger version of that)
I think we should modify the linter to accept cases where the user made it clear he did want the definition to be irreducible in some sense (either with no_expose, or with irreducible_def).

The awkward thing with no_expose is that this only affects the exported declaration. Typically when tagging something as no_expose, you will still rely on unfolding that definition in the file itself. So then it would still need to be tagged with implicit_reducible. But the big problem with this is that downstread users who don't use module, will now have this thing be implicit_reducible that they would rather have as irreducible.
